solution.concept_anchor: Contact metamorphism produces non-foliated rocks under uniform pressure

statement_analysis.statement: Regional (dynamic) metamorphism — Associated with large-scale tectonic activity, operates over vast areas, produces foliated rocks
statement_analysis.reason: Regional metamorphism occurs during orogenic events (mountain building), affecting extensive terrains under directed pressure — it is the primary producer of foliated rocks like schist and gneiss.

statement_analysis.statement: Contact (thermal) metamorphism — Produces strongly foliated rocks due to intense directed pressure around igneous intrusions
statement_analysis.reason: Contact metamorphism involves heat (not directed pressure) from igneous intrusions; it produces NON-foliated rocks (hornfels, marble, quartzite) because uniform confining pressure does not align minerals into foliation.

statement_analysis.statement: Cataclastic metamorphism — Occurs along fault zones due to mechanical crushing and grinding, produces mylonite
statement_analysis.reason: Cataclastic metamorphism results from intense mechanical deformation along fault planes; the product is mylonite (finely crushed, laminated rock) — a less commonly discussed but accurate metamorphic type.

statement_analysis.statement: Hydrothermal metamorphism — Involves chemically active hot fluids altering rock composition, associated with mid-ocean ridge systems
statement_analysis.reason: Hydrothermal metamorphism occurs when hot mineral-laden fluids (often from magmatic activity or seafloor spreading) react with surrounding rocks — mid-ocean ridges are classic sites for this process.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) 'All four' tempts students who know contact metamorphism is a real type and assume it must produce foliated rocks because 'metamorphism generally produces foliated rocks.'
elimination_logic: Pair 1: Regional metamorphism = tectonic + foliation — Correct.
Pair 2: Contact metamorphism involves HEAT not directed pressure; produces NON-foliated rocks — the statement incorrectly says 'strongly foliated due to directed pressure' — Incorrect.
Pair 3: Cataclastic = fault zone + mylonite — Correct.
Pair 4: Hydrothermal = hot fluids + mid-ocean ridges — Correct.
Three pairs are correctly matched → answer is (c) Only three.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Pair 2 exploits the 'all metamorphic rocks are foliated' misconception magnified by 'intense directed pressure' sounding authoritative. In reality, contact metamorphism is driven by HEAT from intrusive bodies — the pressure is uniform (confining), not directed. Uniform pressure does not cause mineral alignment; directed (deviatoric) pressure does. This distinction is the key to understanding why contact metamorphic rocks (hornfels, marble, quartzite) are non-foliated.
solution.final_explanation:
Types of metamorphism differ in agent, scale, and structural outcome.

• Pair 1 — Correct: Regional metamorphism = directed pressure + heat over vast orogenic belts → foliated rocks (schist, gneiss).
• Pair 2 — Incorrect: Contact metamorphism is driven by HEAT from igneous intrusions; pressure is uniform/confining → non-foliated rocks (hornfels around intrusions; marble, quartzite at margins). Foliation requires directed stress, absent in contact settings.
• Pair 3 — Correct: Cataclastic metamorphism = mechanical crushing along fault zones → mylonite (fine-grained, laminated fault rock).
• Pair 4 — Correct: Hydrothermal metamorphism = chemically active fluids reacting with rock → mineral alteration (serpentinisation, chloritisation) — common at mid-ocean ridges.

Value Addition:
• Hornfels is the classic non-foliated contact metamorphic rock — hard, dark, fine-grained.
• The width of a metamorphic aureole around an intrusion depends on the size and temperature of the intrusion.
• Serpentinite (from hydrothermal alteration of peridotite) is geologically important — sometimes hosts asbestos minerals.

solution.concept_anchor: Isostasy — vertical adjustment, density-based buoyancy in mantle

statement_analysis.statement: Granitic continental crust, with a density of approximately 2.7 g/cm³, floats higher in the mantle than basaltic oceanic crust (~3.0 g/cm³) because of its lower density — this forms the physical basis of isostasy.
statement_analysis.reason: Isostasy rests on the density contrast between granitic (felsic, less dense) continental crust and basaltic (mafic, denser) oceanic crust — the buoyancy principle in the plastic mantle explains why continents stand topographically higher. This is correct and NOT the answer.

statement_analysis.statement: Isostatic adjustment and plate tectonics describe the same fundamental crustal movement mechanism, both driven by convection currents in the mantle.
statement_analysis.reason: Isostasy is a vertical equilibrium adjustment (loading/unloading — glaciation, erosion) while plate tectonics involves horizontal movement of lithospheric plates. Though both involve mantle dynamics, they are distinct mechanisms — the statement incorrectly equates them.

statement_analysis.statement: Post-glacial rebound, where the Scandinavian landmass has been rising since the retreat of the last ice sheet, is a documented example of isostatic adjustment.
statement_analysis.reason: Post-glacial rebound (glacial isostatic adjustment) in Scandinavia — where the crust is rising at rates of several mm/year following ice sheet melting — is the most well-documented real-world example of isostasy. This is correct and NOT the answer.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) tempts students who focus on Statement 2 as incorrect but doubt Statement 1, thinking 'isostasy' involves more than just density — leading them to incorrectly mark Statement 1 as also NOT correct.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Granite ~2.7 g/cm³ < Basalt ~3.0 g/cm³; continents float higher — foundational isostasy fact — Statement 1 is Correct (NOT an incorrect statement).
Evaluate Statement 2: Isostasy = vertical adjustment; plate tectonics = lateral movement — equating them is a fundamental error — Statement 2 is INCORRECT.
Evaluate Statement 3: Scandinavian post-glacial rebound is the classic isostasy demonstration — Statement 3 is Correct (NOT an incorrect statement).
Only Statement 2 is NOT correct → answer is (b). Wait — check options: (a) 1 only, (b) 2 only, (c) 1 and 3 only, (d) 2 and 3 only. Statement 2 is the only incorrect one → answer is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges isostasy with plate tectonics — both involve mantle convection broadly, so students who understand one but not the other may accept the equation. The critical distinction: isostasy is a gravitational equilibrium concept (vertical, local-to-regional scale, driven by density/loading changes), while plate tectonics is a kinematic theory of lateral plate movement (global scale, driven by slab pull, ridge push, mantle convection). They coexist but are not the same mechanism.
solution.final_explanation:
Isostasy is the principle of gravitational equilibrium — Earth's crust 'floats' on the mantle in proportion to its density and thickness.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The density contrast (granite 2.7 < basalt 3.0 g/cm³) means continental crust has more buoyancy in the mantle — it stands higher. This is Airy's and Pratt's isostasy models in practice.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect (the answer): Isostasy = vertical equilibrium; plate tectonics = horizontal plate movement. Conflating them misrepresents both concepts. While mantle convection influences plate tectonics, isostatic adjustment is a gravitational response to surface loading/unloading — a separate mechanism.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Scandinavia rises ~5–10 mm/year as the mantle rebounds from the removal of ice sheet weight — the most cited real-world isostasy example.

Value Addition:
• Airy isostasy: thicker crust has deeper roots (mountain roots); Pratt isostasy: different densities at the same depth explain elevation.
• Hudson Bay region (Canada) is still rebounding from Laurentide Ice Sheet melting — another post-glacial rebound site.
• Erosion of mountain ranges leads to isostatic uplift — removing surface load causes the crust to rise, bringing deeper rocks to the surface.

solution.concept_anchor: Diagenesis vs metamorphism — pressure temperature threshold
solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is deceptive because students associate 'compaction and cementation' with the entire post-deposition process, not recognising that diagenesis is the specific technical term, and may choose (d) thinking it is a more complete description.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): 'lithogenesis' is not a standard geological term for this process — it is a plausible fabrication.

Eliminate (b): metamorphism involves much higher temperatures and pressures, resulting in solid-state mineral recrystallisation — diagenesis occurs at lower P-T conditions and does not produce metamorphic minerals.

Eliminate (d): while compaction and cementation are components of diagenesis, describing the entire process as just 'compaction and cementation' misses the full scope of diagenesis (dewatering, mineral dissolution, recrystallisation at low grade).
Confirm (c): diagenesis is the correct specific term for all physical and chemical changes that sediments undergo after deposition but before reaching metamorphic conditions — answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in option (d) limits diagenesis to only 'compaction and cementation,' omitting the broader range of low-temperature chemical changes (dissolution, replacement, mineral precipitation, dewatering) included in diagenesis. Students who have studied lithification as 'compaction + cementation' may choose (d) thinking it captures the process. Option (b) exploits the proximity of diagenesis and metamorphism — both involve post-deposition changes, but metamorphism requires fundamentally higher P-T conditions.
solution.final_explanation:
Diagenesis encompasses all the physical, chemical, and biological changes that sediments undergo after initial deposition but before the conditions required for metamorphism are reached.

• Option (a) — Lithogenesis: Incorrect. This is not a standard scientific term; a plausible-sounding but non-existent technical label.
• Option (b) — Metamorphism: Incorrect. Metamorphism operates at significantly higher temperatures and pressures (typically >150–200°C and >300 MPa) than diagenesis; it involves solid-state mineral recrystallisation into new metamorphic minerals.
• Option (c) — Diagenesis: Correct. The technical term for all post-deposition, pre-metamorphic changes: compaction, dewatering, cementation, dissolution, mineral replacement, and early lithification.
• Option (d) — 'Compaction and cementation' only: Incorrect by scope limitation. While these are the most cited components, diagenesis also includes dewatering, pressure dissolution, and early diagenetic mineral growth.

Value Addition:
• The diagenesis zone ranges from surface to ~5 km depth (temperatures up to ~150–200°C).
• Oil and gas generation begins during late diagenesis — the 'oil window' is a diagenetic phenomenon.
• Chert (microcrystalline silica) often forms diagenetically by replacement of carbonate sediments.

solution.concept_anchor: Pedogenesis sequence from bare rock to mature soil
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) tempts students who place horizon development before organic matter addition, reasoning that 'structure must exist before organisms can colonise.'
elimination_logic: Bare rock must first be physically and chemically broken down by weathering to produce regolith — this is necessarily first.
Pioneer organisms (lichens, mosses) colonise regolith, adding organic matter — biological colonisation follows physical weathering.
Organic matter accumulation creates humus and builds the earliest A-horizon — horizon development (A) follows organic matter addition.
With time, leaching carries minerals downward forming B-horizon, then C-horizon (partially weathered parent material) — mature profile develops last.
Correct sequence: Weathering of bare rock → Regolith formation → Pioneer organism colonisation → Organic matter accumulation → Horizon development → Mature soil profile → option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap targets the 'horizon development vs organic matter' sequence. Students who think soil structure (horizons) must precede biological colonisation may reverse these steps. In reality, horizon development is a consequence of biological activity and leaching over time — pioneer organisms add organic matter first, which then facilitates the development of distinct horizons. No horizon differentiation occurs without prior organic input and chemical leaching.
solution.final_explanation:
Pedogenesis (soil formation) follows a sequence closely tied to the rock cycle, beginning with rock weathering and ending with a mature, stratified soil profile.

Correct sequence: Weathering of bare rock → Regolith (loose mineral material) → Pioneer organisms (lichens, mosses) colonise → Organic matter accumulation → Horizon differentiation → Mature soil profile

• Weathering initiates the process by breaking bedrock into regolith.
• Pioneer organisms (lichens) secrete acids and add organic matter, transforming regolith into proto-soil.
• Organic matter creates humus, improving water retention and enabling further biological activity.
• Leaching and chemical processes differentiate regolith into distinct horizons (O, A, B, C layers).
• A mature soil profile with all horizons represents the end-product of pedogenesis.

Why other options fail: Options placing horizon development before organic matter addition, or regolith formation before weathering, contradict the physical logic of pedogenesis.

Value Addition:
• Jenny's CLORPT: Climate (most important), Organisms, Relief, Parent rock, Time — the five soil-forming factors.
• Laterisation (tropical leaching of silica) and Podzolisation (temperate leaching of iron/aluminium) are two distinct pedogenic pathways.
• Residual soils develop above parent rock; transported soils (alluvial, colluvial) are carried from elsewhere.

solution.concept_anchor: Unconformities — types and Indian stratigraphic significance

statement_analysis.statement: An angular unconformity records a sequence of events including deposition of older strata, their folding or tilting, uplift and erosion, and then renewed horizontal deposition — representing multiple phases of the rock cycle.
statement_analysis.reason: Angular unconformity captures a complete rock cycle episode: deposition → tectonic deformation → erosion → renewed deposition; it is a multi-phase geological record, accurately described.

statement_analysis.statement: Biostratigraphy uses fossils found in sedimentary rocks above and below unconformities to estimate the duration of the time gap they represent.
statement_analysis.reason: By comparing fossil assemblages (biostratigraphic zones) in rocks immediately above and below an unconformity, geologists can estimate how much geological time is missing — this is a standard stratigraphic technique.

statement_analysis.statement: The Vindhyan Supergroup of central India is a thick sequence of igneous and metamorphic rocks deposited after the Archaean crystalline basement, making it the second-oldest rock unit in India.
statement_analysis.reason: The Vindhyan Supergroup is a thick SEDIMENTARY sequence (sandstone, limestone, shale) overlying the Archaean crystalline basement — it is not igneous or metamorphic. Describing it as igneous/metamorphic is factually incorrect.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) 'All three' tempts students who know both the unconformity process (Statement 1) and biostratigraphy (Statement 2) are correct and assume the Vindhyan description (Statement 3) must also be right because the Vindhyan Supergroup is genuinely ancient.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Angular unconformity records deformation → erosion → renewed deposition — multi-phase rock cycle record — Correct.
Statement 2: Biostratigraphy using fossils across unconformity surfaces to quantify time gaps — standard geological technique — Correct.
Statement 3: Vindhyan Supergroup described as 'igneous and metamorphic' — this is wrong; it is a sedimentary sequence — Incorrect.
Statements 1 and 2 correct, Statement 3 incorrect → answer is (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 contains a partial-truth trap — the Vindhyan Supergroup is genuinely ancient and overlies the Archaean crystalline basement (both parts true), but its rock type is mischaracterised as 'igneous and metamorphic.' The Vindhyan is a classic sedimentary succession (sandstone, shale, limestone). Students who know the Vindhyan name and its Proterozoic age may accept the rock type description without precise recall, especially when the surrounding context (Statement 1 and 2) is accurate.
solution.final_explanation:
Unconformities and stratigraphy are tools for reading the rock cycle record through geological time.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Angular unconformity is a textbook record of rock cycle phases — sedimentation, tectonics, erosion, renewed sedimentation. James Hutton's discovery at Siccar Point demonstrated this sequence.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Fossils provide biostratigraphic control — comparing zones above and below unconformities quantifies missing time. Combined with radiometric dating, this builds the geological timescale.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The Vindhyan Supergroup is a thick sedimentary sequence (shale, sandstone, limestone) of Proterozoic age (~1.7–0.5 Ga), NOT igneous or metamorphic. It is economically significant for diamond-bearing Kimberlite pipes and building stone.

Value Addition:
• The 'Great Unconformity' represents ~1 billion years missing from the geological record — globally significant.
• Vindhyan rocks extend across Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, and Uttar Pradesh — the Son Valley exposures are famous.
• Panna diamond fields (Madhya Pradesh) are associated with Kimberlite intrusions cutting through Vindhyan sedimentary rocks.

solution.concept_anchor: Magma vs lava distinction — subsurface vs surface molten rock
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because magmatic differentiation is a real process (fractional crystallisation) but the statement claims it produces only one rock type from a single magma body, which is the opposite of what differentiation means.
elimination_logic: Evaluate (a): Magma = subsurface molten rock; Lava = magma that has reached the surface — this fundamental distinction is correctly stated.
Evaluate (b): Magmatic differentiation produces MULTIPLE rock types from a single magma body through fractional crystallisation — the statement incorrectly says 'only one rock type.'

Evaluate (c): Subduction zones produce andesitic/rhyolitic magma (water-rich, silica-rich from subducted oceanic crust + overlying mantle wedge) — not purely basaltic; mid-ocean ridges produce basaltic — the pairs are swapped.
Evaluate (d): Basaltic magma is silica-POOR and erupts effusively (fluid, non-explosive) — the statement incorrectly attributes explosive eruptions to basaltic magma.
Only (a) is correctly matched → answer is (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (c) contains a classic entity-swap — subduction zones and mid-ocean ridges are swapped in their magma type associations. Students who recall 'subduction = basaltic' (incorrect — subduction produces andesitic) may accept (c). Mid-ocean ridge magma is generated by decompression melting of the mantle — it produces basaltic magma. Subduction zone magma is generated by flux melting (water from subducted slab lowers melting point) in a silica-richer, water-richer environment, producing andesitic to rhyolitic magma.
solution.final_explanation:
The magma-lava-rock relationship is foundational to understanding the igneous component of the rock cycle.

• Option (a) — Correct: Magma is molten rock beneath the surface; lava is the same material after it reaches the Earth's surface. This distinction determines whether the resulting rock is intrusive (plutonic) or extrusive (volcanic).
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Magmatic differentiation produces MULTIPLE rock types from a single parent magma — early-forming high-temperature minerals crystallise first, leaving behind a progressively evolved (more silica-rich) residual melt that can generate different rock types.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Subduction zones produce andesitic to rhyolitic (silica-rich) magma; mid-ocean ridges produce basaltic (silica-poor) magma from decompression melting — the statement reverses these associations.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Basaltic magma has LOW silica, is non-viscous, and erupts effusively — NOT explosively. Explosive eruptions characterise high-silica rhyolitic magma.

Value Addition:
• Bowen's Reaction Series explains the sequence of mineral crystallisation as magma cools — foundation of magmatic differentiation.
• Hawaiian eruptions (basaltic, effusive) vs Pinatubo 1991 eruption (andesitic-rhyolitic, explosive) — contrasting magma types.
• Vesicles in extrusive rocks = gas bubble cavities; when filled with minerals = amygdules.

solution.concept_anchor: Collision zones produce regional metamorphic rocks — Himalayan terrain
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is the strongest distractor because the Himalayas are genuinely fold mountains formed by collision, and students may select 'contact metamorphism' thinking that the intense collision produced localised heat effects, without recognising that collision-zone metamorphism is REGIONAL, not contact.
elimination_logic: The scenario describes two continents colliding, creating a mountain belt — this is an orogenic collision zone.
Orogenic collision generates high pressure AND temperature over a vast region — the defining conditions of regional (dynamic) metamorphism.

Eliminate (a): contact metamorphism is localised around igneous intrusions — it is small-scale and heat-driven; collision zones involve directed pressure over vast areas, not localised intrusive heat.
Eliminate (b): seafloor spreading is a divergent process producing NEW basaltic crust — the opposite of collision; this scenario is convergent.

Eliminate (d): cataclastic metamorphism occurs along fault planes through crushing — while faults exist in collision zones, the widespread high-P-T metamorphism over the entire orogen is regional, not cataclastic.
Confirm (c): continental collision = regional (dynamic) metamorphism over a vast orogenic belt — produces schist, gneiss, eclogite.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (a) is the partial-truth trap — contact metamorphism does involve heat, and collision zones do generate heat. But contact metamorphism is specifically the localised thermal alteration around igneous intrusions (within metres to kilometres), not the vast pressure-dominated regional metamorphism of orogenic belts spanning hundreds of kilometres. The collision scenario in the question specifically generates DIRECTED pressure and elevated temperatures over a vast region — the diagnostic signature of regional metamorphism.
solution.final_explanation:
Continental collision at convergent plate boundaries generates the conditions for regional (orogenic) metamorphism — the most areally extensive type of metamorphism.

When two continental plates collide (as India-Eurasia did ~50 Ma ago), the crust thickens dramatically. Burial of rocks under kilometres of overriding crust generates both high pressure (lithostatic + directed tectonic stress) and elevated temperature over a vast region. This produces a systematic zonation of metamorphic rocks — from low-grade chlorite/slate at the margins to high-grade gneiss/eclogite in the core.

• Option (a): Incorrect — Contact metamorphism is localised around intrusions; it is heat-driven and small-scale (aureoles of metres to kilometres), not the orogenic scale described.
• Option (b): Incorrect — Seafloor spreading is divergent; it creates new basaltic crust, not collision-zone metamorphics.
• Option (c): Correct — Continental collision generates regional (dynamic) metamorphism: directed pressure + elevated temperature over vast orogenic belts → schist, gneiss, eclogite.
• Option (d): Incorrect — Cataclastic metamorphism is mechanical crushing along fault zones; it is localised and does not explain the broad metamorphic terrains of orogenic belts.

Value Addition:
• The Himalayan Central Crystallines (Greater Himalayas) are a classic regional metamorphic belt.
• Eclogite (high-pressure, high-temperature metamorphic rock) indicates subducted continental crust brought back to the surface.
• Blueschist facies rocks indicate high-pressure, low-temperature metamorphism at subduction zones — different from collision-zone conditions.

(d) Cataclastic metamorphism along individual fault planes, which crushed pre-existing rocks into the observed high-grade assemblages

solution.concept_anchor: Rock cycle comparison with water and carbon cycles

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 1: Unlike the water cycle, which operates primarily through physical phase changes of H₂O, the rock cycle involves transformations in mineral composition, crystal structure, and texture — making it a fundamentally different type of geochemical cycle.
statement_analysis.reason: The rock cycle involves chemical and structural transformations of silicate minerals under variable P-T conditions — qualitatively different from the water cycle's phase-change mechanism (evaporation, condensation, precipitation), even though both cycle matter through the Earth system.

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 2: The carbon cycle intersects with the rock cycle exclusively through biological processes such as photosynthesis and respiration, with no involvement of abiotic geological mechanisms.
statement_analysis.reason: The carbon-silicate cycle (silicate rock weathering consuming CO₂), carbonate rock formation (geological carbon storage), and volcanic outgassing (returning CO₂ to the atmosphere) are all abiotic geological mechanisms where the carbon cycle and rock cycle intersect — biological processes are not the exclusive intersection point.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students may select (a) 'both correct' by verifying Statement 1 accurately and then accepting Statement 2 based on familiarity with photosynthesis-respiration as THE carbon cycle mechanism, without recalling the geological (abiotic) carbon-rock cycle connections.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: rock cycle = mineral composition + crystal structure transformation ≠ water cycle's physical phase changes — distinction is valid — Statement 1 is Correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: 'exclusively through biological processes' — the carbon-silicate cycle (abiotic silicate weathering consuming CO₂), limestone formation, and volcanism are abiotic rock-carbon cycle intersections — the word 'exclusively' makes Statement 2 false.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect → answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 uses 'exclusively' — a classic scope-extension qualifier. Students trained on the biological carbon cycle (photosynthesis-respiration loop) may not recall or may underweight the geological carbon cycle (silicate weathering → carbonate rock formation → volcanism). The reversed-causation element is subtle: students may think 'geology affects biology (carbon) but not the reverse' and accept Statement 2 without realising that abiotic geological processes are the DOMINANT long-term carbon cycle mechanisms.
solution.final_explanation:
The rock cycle, water cycle, and carbon cycle interact across multiple timescales but operate through fundamentally different mechanisms.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The rock cycle involves mineralogical, crystallographic, and textural transformations — silicate minerals are restructured by heat, pressure, and chemical fluids. The water cycle involves only physical phase changes (solid-liquid-gas) of the same molecule. They are distinct cycle types despite both cycling matter through the Earth system.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The carbon cycle intersects the rock cycle through several abiotic pathways: (i) silicate weathering consuming CO₂ (Urey reaction), (ii) carbonate rock formation (limestone as geological carbon store), and (iii) volcanic degassing returning CO₂. Biological processes are one intersection but definitely not the exclusive one.

Value Addition:
• Over geological timescales (millions of years), the geological carbon cycle dominates; biological carbon cycle operates over years-to-decades.
• The carbon cycle, water cycle, and rock cycle together constitute the major biogeochemical cycles driving Earth system function.
• Comparing cycle timescales: water cycle ~9 days; biological carbon cycle ~decades; geological rock cycle ~millions of years.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is deceptive because it correctly pairs Gondwana formations with coal but incorrectly assigns the Deccan Traps to metamorphic rocks, trapping students who know one pair precisely but not the others.
